case_info.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

options.C: Advise patient that family members are at risk for pattern dystrophy

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Prompt the clinician to walk through what they see as the most compelling evidence linking pentosan polysulfate to the retinal changes, and what they consider the least acceptable risk to justify discontinuation.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')",
  "confidence": "a number from 0 to 1 for how confident you are that your stated belief is

}

[Role]

about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:

Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. 1 = Very low workload

5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

[Clinical case]
A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

[Clinical case]
A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

case_info.explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands.
